title: Practice Set 2
text:
In this practice set, we’ll learn how to load data in R and describe a single variable using a real dataset from Pan and Siegel (2019), “How Saudi Crackdowns Fail to Silence Online Dissent,” published in the American Political Science Review. The authors study how governments use offline tactics, like imprisonment, to punish online activism. To do this, they examine what happens after well-known Saudis are jailed for online dissent, analyzing over 300 million tweets posted between 2010 and 2017.
We want to know if activists tweeted less after they were released from prison.

Restate this as a testable hypothesis.







Answer





In a comparison of days before Saudi activists’ arrest and days after their release, the activists will post fewer total tweets per day after release than before.




What is being compared?







Answer





Daily tweet volume for the group of activists in the year before arrest vs. the year after release.




What is the IV and DV?







Answer





IV: Whether a day is before arrest or after release (post_release), DV: Total number of tweets the group posted that day (tweets)




What is the unit of analysis?







Answer





The day (relative to arrest/release). Each row is one day’s total tweets for the whole group, not one activist.





Download the dataset here
Each row in this dataset records the number of tweets a well-known Saudi posted on a single day, covering the year before their arrest and the year after their release. The post_release column tells you which period a row falls in: it equals 0 for days before the arrest and 1 for days after the release. The days_post_release column tells you which specific day it is. Negative values count days before the arrest, so -365 is exactly one year before and -100 is 100 days before. Positive values count days after the release, so 100 is 100 days after they got out.
You must run the below code first to work through these problems on this site.

title: Practice Set 2
text:
Definitions

What is a package in R?







Answer





A bundle of functions, data, and documentation that someone else wrote to extend what R can do (e.g., tidyverse for data wrangling and plotting)




What does it mean to load a dataframe into R?







Answer





Reading a data file (like a .csv) from your computer into your R session and saving it as an object you can work with, e.g., df <- read_csv(“file.csv”).




Is there a difference between loading and installing a package? If so, what is the difference, and how does this affect how you code in R?







Answer





Yes, they’re different. - Installing (install.packages(“tidyverse”)) downloads the package to your computer. You only do this once, and you shouldn’t leave it in your script. - Loading (library(tidyverse)) makes the package available in your current session. You do this every time you start R, so put it at the top of your script.

title: Practice Set 2
text:
Working Directory
Run getwd() in your R session.









What is this output?







Answer





The file path of your current working directory, which is the folder R looks in by default for files to read and save to.




What does the function setwd() do?







Answer





It changes the working directory to whatever folder path you give it.




You’re helping your friend with R, and after they run getwd() they get the below output. What does this tell us?


  /Users/student/Desktop






Answer





Their working directory is currently their Desktop, so R will look for files there.




What happens when they run

  setwd("/Users/student/Desktop/comm_106")






Answer





The working directory changes to the comm_106 folder on their Desktop, as long as that folder exists. If it doesn’t exist, they’ll get an error.




After your friend has set their working directory, they download arrested_tweet_volume.csv from this site. Can they start working with this dataset in R now?







Answer





No.  - The file probably went to their Downloads folder, not comm_106. They need to move it into comm_106 or use its full file path. - Downloading isn’t the same as loading. They still need to read it in, e.g., df <- read_csv(“arrested_tweet_volume.csv”).




Reading in Data
Change the code below in order to generate the following error messages. Briefly describe why your change causes this error to show up.











    Error in read_csv("arrested_tweet_volume.csv") : could not find function "read_csv"






Answer













Without `library(tidyverse)`, the package that contains `read_csv()` never gets loaded, so R doesn't know the function exists.






    Error:
    ! "arrest_tweet_volume.csv" does not exist in current working directory






Answer













The name of the csv file is wrong, the error says it can’t find a arrest_tweet_volume.csv, which doesn’t exist.






    Error: object 'arrested_tweet_volume.csv' not found






Answer













Without quotation marks, R treats arrested_tweet_volume.csv as the name of an object in your environment instead of a file name. No object has that name, so R says it’s not found.





Load Data in Your Own R Session
If you haven’t already, download the dataset here, and load it in.

What are the dimensions of this dataframe?







Answer





730 by 3












How many rows are in this dataframe?







Answer





730 rows. We also can see this from dim(), which outputs rows X columns, so we have 3 columns.












What are the names of the dataframe’s columns?







Answer





“tweets”, “post_release”, days_post_release” 730 rows. We also can see this from dim(), which outputs rows X columns, so we have 3 columns.

title: Practice Set 2
text:
Variable Type

Is tweets a nominal, ordinal, or interval variable?







Answer





Interval. Tweets is a count of tweets, so the numbers have equal spacing and a meaningful order (10 tweets is exactly 5 more than 5 tweets).




Find the mean, minimum, maximum, and median of tweets using the summary() function







Answer





Mean: 209.8 Median: 192.0 Min: 21.0 Max: 726.0












Interpret the statistics in terms of the study context.







Answer





Mean: On average, the group of activists posted 210 (rounded up from 209.8) tweets per day. Median: On half of the days the group posted fewer than 192 tweets, and on half they posted more. Min/Max: The group’s quietest day had 21 tweets and its busiest day had 726 tweets.




Are these statistics meaningful analysis for tweets? What are the appropriate analyses for tweets?







Answer





Yes. Because tweets is interval, means, medians, and ranges all make sense. Other appropriate analyses include the standard deviation and the IQR to describe spread. Since tweet counts are usually skewed, the median and IQR are often a better summary than the mean and SD.




What are the appropriate visualizations for tweets?







Answer





A histogram shows the shape of the distribution. A boxplot shows the median, spread, and outliers. Bar charts aren’t a good fit, since those are for nominal and ordinal variables.



Repeat 1-5 with post_release and days_post_release






post_release Answer






Nominal. It’s a binary (dummy) variable: 1 means after release and 0 means before arrest. The numbers are labels for two categories, not amounts.
Mean: 0.5 Median: 0.5 Min: 0 Max: 1










Mean: Usually, we don’t calculate means for nominal variables. However, since the variable is either 0 or 1, the mean tells us the proportion of observations that are after release – half, which we already know, since we designed the data to be that way. Median: Half of the variables in this dataset are less than or equal to 0.5 and the other half is greater or equal to than 0.5. Min/Max: These will be 0 and 1, which just confirms both categories are in the data.
No. We created post_release ourselves by splitting the study window in two: days after release are 1 and days before arrest are 0. Since the window covers the same number of days on each side, we already know half the days will be 1s, so the mean is 0.5. We also know the min is 0 and the max is 1. These statistics just reflect how we built the variable, not anything about how the activists behaved. They’re still useful as a check that the variable was coded correctly, e.g., with table(df$post_release). The real use of post_release is as the IV: grouping the days by it to compare tweets before and after.
A possible visualization for nominal variables is a bar chart showing the number or share of observations in each category. However, it isn’t appropriate because we already know what it will look like.










days_post_release Answer






Interval. It counts days relative to the activists’ arrest/release, running from -365 (one year before) to 365 (one year after). The spacing is equal and the order is meaningful. Negative values are fine for an interval variable, since -30 to -20 is the same 10-day gap as 20 to 30.
Mean: 0 Median: 0 Min: -365 Max: 365










Mean: The average day is 0. Median: The middle day is also 0. Min/Max: The data runs from -365 to 365, so it covers one year before and one year after. The mean and median are both 0 because there’s the same number of days on each side of 0. They tell us the study window is balanced, not anything about the activists.
No. Since each day appears exactly once, these statistics describe how the study was designed (how much time it covers) rather than anything we measured.
It’s possible to show the visualizations appropriate for interval variables, but none of them are appropriate. We know that every day appears once, so a histogram would be flat.





Below, we create a new variable that sorts each day into an activity level.










What level of measurement is activity? What does class(activity) return?







Answer





Ordinal. The categories have a clear order (silent < low < medium < high), but the gaps between them aren’t equal: “silent” is exactly 0 tweets, while “low” covers 1–49. class(activity) returns “character”, because case_when() outputs text labels.




Why does mean() return NA? Read the warning.







Answer





mean() only works on numeric or logical values, and activity is a character vector. R can’t average words, so it returns NA with the warning argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA.




Even if R could compute a mean here, would it be meaningful? What summary would you use instead?







Answer





No. Even if we coded the categories as 1–4, a mean would assume the gaps between levels are equal, and they aren’t. Better summaries are counts and proportions for each level, e.g., table(activity), and the mode or median category.

title: Practice Set 2
text:
Center and Spread

Your research assistant tells you that they made an error with data entry – they forgot to add a 0 to the end of the 5 largest number of tweets in the dataset; e.g. 726 should actually be 7260. This could change everything!

We update our dataframe from df to df_updated (You don’t have to worry about knowing how to do this yet)








How does this change affect the:

Median







Answer





  Median: Doesn't change. Only the top 5 values change, and they were already above the median, so the middle value stays the same.




Interquartile Range







Answer





  IQR: Doesn't change. The top 5 days are all above the 75th percentile, so Q1 and Q3 stay the same.




Mode







Answer





  Mode: Doesn't change. The most common value is very unlikely to be one of the 5 biggest days.




Mean







Answer





  Mean: Goes up. The mean uses every value, so a few very large days pull it up.




Range







Answer





  Range: Goes up a lot. The max is now 10 times bigger, so the range (max − min) is much wider.



*Hint: Try rerunning the above exercises with df_updated instead of df

You’re now unsure on whether or not your research assistant knows what they’re talking about. When you hired your assistant, they had taken 6 statistics classes in high school with the following grades: 93, 97, 98, 92, 90, 90. Since then, they’ve taken their first undergraduate-level statistics class, and you check their transcript to see what grade they got – a 53!

Which summary do you expect to change the most, and why?

Median
Interquartile Range
Mode
Mean
Range







Answer






Range The range depends only on the most extreme values, so a single outlier can change it a lot. The mean moves too, but less, because the 53 is averaged in with six other grades.





You’ve decided to fire your assistant, and you need to give them a reason. You want to use their statistics grades (93, 97, 98, 92, 90, 90, 53) to back up your decision.


Would the mean or the median make a stronger case for firing them? Why?







Answer





The mean. The mean is 87.6, while the median is 92. The mean is pulled down by the 53 because it uses every value, so it makes the assistant look worse. The median ignores how extreme the 53 is, so it still looks like an A-range student.




Which summary gives a fairer picture of their typical performance? Is it fair to fire them based on these grades?







Answer





The median. Six of their seven (haha) grades are 90 or above, and the median reflects that typical performance. The mean is dragged down by a single outlier. So using the mean to justify firing would be picking the statistic that best supports the conclusion you already wanted. A fairer argument would point to the 53 directly: it’s their most recent grade, and the only one from a college-level class, so it may be the most relevant. Neither the mean nor the median captures that, because summaries ignore the order of grades over time.

Filtering Rows

Use the filter() function to filter the dataframe df, and output the dimensions for each filtered dataframe.

The value in post_release is 0








Answer

















The value in post_release is not 0







Answer

















The value in days_post_release is between -100 and 100







Answer

















The value in tweets is less than 100







Answer

















The value in tweets is less than 100 and the value in post_release is 1







Answer

















The value in tweets is less than 100 and the value in post_release is 0







Answer

















The value in post_release is 2.







Answer

















We know that the only values in post_release are either 0 or 1. You didn’t get an error when you did part g, so what happened?

What are the dimensions of the result?








Answer





The result has 0 rows and the same number of columns as df. If df has just tweets, post_release, and days_post_release, dim() returns 0X3. filter() drops rows but never columns, so the columns are still there, just with nothing in them.




Why didn’t R complain?







Answer





filter() checks post_release == 2 for every row and keeps the rows where it’s TRUE. Here the answer is FALSE for every row, so no rows are kept. As far as R is concerned, “no rows match” is a perfectly valid result, and R doesn’t know which values you expected to find. This is why it’s a good habit to check your results with dim() or nrow(): some mistakes don’t produce an error and just give you the wrong answer quietly.

text:
Understanding Error Messages
Run each chunk below. Explain what went wrong, then fix the code.

















Answer





= assigns a value, and == checks whether two things are equal. filter() needs a condition that’s TRUE or FALSE for each row, so it needs ==.




















Answer





R is case-sensitive, so Tweets and tweets are different names. There’s no column called Tweets, so R gives the error Column Tweets doesn't exist.




















Answer





The pipe %>% is missing at the end of the first line. Without it, R runs df %>% filter(post_release == 0) as one complete command and prints the result. Then it tries to run pull(tweets) on its own, which gives an error, since pull() doesn’t know which dataframe to use.




















Answer





The column is called tweets, not tweet. Since there’s no column called tweet, df$tweet returns NULL with the warning Unknown or uninitialised column. mean() can’t average nothing, so it returns NA. Like part g above, it doesn’t stop with an error, so it’s easy to miss.

title: Practice Set 2
text:
Before vs. After Release: Means
We want to know if activists tweeted less after they were released from prison.

Find the mean of tweets of the rows where post_release is 0.







Answer

















Find the mean of tweets of the rows where post_release is 1.







Answer

















Doing it all in one shot

Write one pipeline that

reads in the CSV
keeps only rows where post_release is 0
selects the tweets column
pulls it out as a vector
Runs summary() on the vector

Your pipeline counts as one pipeline if:

it starts by reading in the CSV, and every step after that is connected with %>%
there’s no <- anywhere. You never save the data, or anything else, to an object along the way
df never appears. The data gets passed from step to step by the pipe, not by name
running it prints the summary directly








Answer

















Now swap summary() for mean() and delete the pull() step. What happens, and why?







Answer





R returns NA with the warning argument is not numeric or logical: returning NA. Without pull(), the last step passes a dataframe to mean(), not a numeric vector. select() keeps the data as a dataframe, even with just one column, while pull() takes the column out as a vector. mean() only works on numeric or logical vectors, so it can’t average a dataframe. To fix it, put pull(tweets) back in before mean().













Interpretation

Describe the comparison between 1 and 2 in plain terms, as if you were describing it to your friend.







Answer





Before they were arrested, the activists posted about 304 tweets a day as a group. After they got out of prison, that dropped to about 115 tweets a day. So they were tweeting roughly a third as much as before, about a 62% drop. It looks like, on average, going to prison is associated with activists being quieter online afterwards.

title: Practice Set 2
text:
Before vs. After Release: Spread

Standard Deviation Concepts

Before their arrest, Activist A posts about 15 tweets nearly every day. After their release, they post nothing on most days, then 100+ on days when something big happens. In both periods, they average about 15 tweets a day.


In which period do Activist A’s daily tweet counts have the larger standard deviation?







Answer





Before they were arrested, the activists posted about 304 tweets a day as a group. After they got out of prison, that dropped to about 115 tweets a day. So they were tweeting roughly a third as much as before, about a 62% drop. It looks like, on average, going to prison is associated with activists being quieter online afterwards.




If you only looked at the mean, what would you conclude about how Activist A’s tweeting changed? What does the standard deviation add?







Answer





Looking only at the mean, you’d conclude nothing changed, since Activist A averages 15 tweets a day in both periods. The standard deviation shows that their behavior did change: they went from tweeting steadily every day to staying quiet most of the time and speaking up only when something big happens. Two periods can have the same mean but very different patterns, so it’s important to look at spread as well as the center.




How does standard deviation relate to the mean?







Answer





The standard deviation measures how far the values usually are from the mean. The mean tells us where the center of the data is, and the SD tells us how spread out the values are around that center. A small SD means most values are close to the mean, and a large SD means many values are far from it. Both are in the same units as the variable, so here the SD is measured in tweets per day.





Standard Deviation Calculation

Find the standard deviation of tweets of the rows where post_release is 0.







Answer

















Find the standard deviation of tweets of the rows where post_release is 1.







Answer

















Is the number of tweets more evenly spread before or after release? How can you tell?







Answer





The period with the smaller SD has more evenly spread tweets, since its days are closer to the average. Here, after release has the smaller SD (58.329 vs. 96.732), so the group’s daily tweet counts were more consistent in that period. Keep in mind that the means are very different (304 before vs. 115 after). Smaller numbers tend to have smaller SDs, so part of the difference in SD may just come from tweeting less overall, not from tweeting more evenly. In the coming weeks, we’ll learn how to tell whether a difference like this is real or could just be due to chance.




What are the appropriate visualizations?







Answer





To compare the distribution of tweets before and after, use side-by-side boxplots (one for each value of post_release) or histograms split by post_release. These show both the center and the spread for each period.




In this analysis, we didn’t use days_post_release. Why might we want to include it, and what analyses does it license us to do?







Answer





post_release only tells us whether a day is before or after, so comparing the two means treats every day in a period the same – tweets from a year before arrest and one day before arrest both get a value of 0. days_post_release tells us when each day happened, which lets us look at change over time. For example, we can: - Plot tweets over days_post_release to see whether the drop happens right after release or gradually. - Check whether tweeting was already declining before the arrest. If it was, the drop after release might not be caused by prison. - See whether tweeting recovers as more time passes after release - an activists could stop tweeting the first 100 days after their arrest, but then go back to normal levels. - Compare shorter windows, like the 100 days before and after, to focus on the period closest to the arrest.

title: Histograms
text: To work through questions of distribution, we’ll use the dataset from Bertrand & Mullainathan’s 2004 study, “Are Emily and Greg More Employable Than Lakisha and Jamal? A Field Experiment on Labor Market Discrimination”. In this study, the authors sent out 4870 fake resumes, which they had randomly assigned to have either an African-American or White sounding name. They found that White names receive 50 percent more callbacks for interviews. The dataset, which you can download locally here, lists every resume and the job it was sent to.

title: Histograms
text:
Interpretation
Looking at the visual, we can see that the resumes are not uniformly distributed across years of experience, and that resumes generally have less years of experience.

title: Histograms
text:
Occupation
To think through this, we’ll make a bar plot for the occup_broad column, which categorizes the jobs a resume applied to into Executive, Administrative, Sales representatives, Sales workers, Secretaries, and Clerical. This makes it a nominal variable.








Compare this plot to the years of experience plot. In a histogram, the overall shape of the data tells us what the distribution of the data is, we can learn something about the data when our eyes move across the x-axis. In a bar plot of a nominal variable, the order of the x-axis doesn’t matter. You can rearrange the categories however you want and you’ll still have the same information. In the histogram, we can see that as years of experience increases, the less resumes there are.

title: Histograms
text:
Education
education lists the highest level of education reported on each resume, which ranges from: 1 = high school dropout; 2 = high school graduate; 3 = some college; 4 = College graduate or more, (and 0 for not reported). This makes it an ordinal variable, because the order of the categories matter.








At first glance, this seems to function very similarly as the years of experience histogram – we can see that (whatever distribution pattern)
However, the intervals on the x-axis are not equal. From the perspective of someone reading the resume, we can imagine that there is some difference in the evaluation of high school dropout applicants and high school graduate applicants. But is this difference the same as how someone with some college is compared to someone with a high school graduate?
More importantly, you can tell very different stories with the same data based on how you create categories, or even just choosing bin width.

title: Changing the Dataframe
text:
if_else()
We can also use conditional statements to generate new columns. Let’s say we want a column that indicates whether a passenger was an adult (Age >= 18)
We can use the if_else() function, which requires three inputs, in this order: (1) the condition (2) the value if the condition is met (3) the value if the condition is not met.









Dealing with unknown values
You may notice that some values in Is_Adult column are neither “Yes” or “No”, but something called NA instead. We get this value when the value in Age was missing, so R can’t determine whether or not the value is greater or equal to 18.
We can deal with this by adding another input into the if_else() function: missing = "Unknown"








Now, instead of NA as the value, the missing values will have an actual value.

title: Data Manipulation
text: Now that you’ve loaded a dataframe in, here’s some stuff we can do with it

title: Vectors and Vector Operations
text: We now know about the Numerics, Logicals, and Character classes; that we can use functions on these objects; and we can assign variable names to objects.

title: Vectors and Vector Operations
text:
Vectors
A vector is a set of values of the same type. You can think of it like a column on a spreadsheet. We can make a vector with the c() function.








All the elements in a vector need to be the same datatype, there are some functions that work on entire vectors.
We can get the mean, or average, number of Red Bulls I drink every week for the last 6 weeks by using the mean() function.








Note that every element in redbulls_drank is of the numeric type. We can also do things with vectors filled with characters. The toupper() function turns every character into uppercase.








However, it wouldn’t make sense to try to get the mean of my favorite flavors. Nor would it make sense to try to uppercase numbers.








It also wouldn’t make sense to get the mean of the number of Red Bulls I drank and my favorite flavors.








This doesn’t mean that numeric vectors can only use numeric vector functions, that logical vectors can only use logical vector functions, and so on. The length() function tells you how many elements are in a vector, and works on all kinds of vectors, and the unique() function tells you how many unique values are in a vector.








You can also access a specific element in a vector based on its position. In redbull_flavor, “cherry” has a position of 1, “lime” has a position of 2, “apple” has a position of 3, and “strawberry” has a position of 4. We can refer to a specific element by: redbull_flavor[1], which is “cherry”









Vector to Vector Operations
We can work with multiple vectors. We’ll make a new numeric vector that lists the number of cups of water I drank each week for the past 6 weeks.








We can get a new vector by adding redbulls_drank to waters_drank using the same numeric operation rules for numerics.

title: Logistic Regression
text:
Linear regressions allow us to model the real world, and importantly also allow us to predict what would happen in scenarios that haven’t occurred. While this is comforting, they don’t actually allow us to see into the future. Confidence intervals and p-values remind us that a linear regression is ultimately an estimate, not a certainty.
Remember what a p-value of 0.05 (the standard threshold) means: if there were truly no relationship, we’d still get a result at least as extreme as ours in about 5 out of 100 samples.
That’s pretty unlikely, which is why we treat it as evidence. But unlikely isn’t impossible. Stanford’s undergraduate admission rate was 3.6%, even lower than 5%, and yet thousands of students get in every year. Rare things happen all the time, especially when there are lots of chances for them to happen.
The same goes for research: if 20 researchers each test a relationship that doesn’t actually exist, we’d expect about one of them to get p < 0.05 by chance alone.
Another pitfall of reading linear regression results too literally is that the model will happily make predictions about situations that are unlikely or even impossible in the real world. For example, we might find that people are more likely to own a home as they get older. But the same model will also give us a prediction for someone who is 200 years old, or -5 years old.
Issues like this are why the work on quantitative social science methods is so deep and active… and thrilling!

Logistic Regression
One extension of linear regression is logistic regression, which addresses the problem of predicting probabilities. Your chance of owning a home can only be between 0 and 1 (or 0% and 100%), and a logistic regression makes sure its predictions stay in that range.
We’ll use Bonica 2024’s Database on Ideology, Money in Elections (DIME), which you can download locally here, which contains 8948 observations of donations from PACs (Political Action Committees) received by candidates in US elections from 1979 to 2024. Each candidate is also measured on how extreme their ideology (Left to Right) is.








Existing work suggests that PACs tend to support more moderate candidates. We can set up a logistic regression to answer how likely a candidate is to be extreme, given how much PAC money they received.


Hypothesis

In a comparison of candidates, those who received more money from PACs were less likely to be ideologically extreme than those who received less money from PACs.

Identify the Null

\(H_0\) : Receiving more PAC money does not decrease a candidate’s likelihood of being ideologically extreme. In other words, the coefficient on PAC receipts is greater than or equal to zero (\(\beta \geq 0\)).

Identify the appropriate test statistic

Our dependent variable (extreme) is 0-1 and our independent variable (log_pac_receipts) is interval, so we use logistic regression. Logistic regression reports a z-statistic instead of a t-statistic, but we read it the same way: it tells us how many standard errors the coefficient is from zero.

Calculate the z-statistic

glm() works like lm(), but it can handle outcomes that aren’t interval variables. family = binomial tells R that our outcome is 0-1.









Evaluate p-value

Look at the log_pac_receipts row of the coefficients table. The z value column is the z-statistic, and Pr(>|z|) is the p-value.
Pr(>|z|) is a two-sided p-value. Since our hypothesis is one-sided, if the coefficient is negative (the direction we predicted), we can divide this p-value by 2.
A negative coefficient means candidates who received more PAC money were less likely to be extreme.

Report results

Because logistic regression coefficients are in log-odds, we convert them into predicted probabilities to describe the size of the relationship. Here, we compare a candidate at the 25th percentile of PAC receipts to one at the 75th percentile:
















Result



Candidates who received more PAC money were less likely to be ideologically extreme. Moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile of PAC receipts is associated with a change in the predicted probability of being extreme from 80.993% to 72.103%. This relationship is statistically significant (p<0.001)

title: Comparison of Means
text:
Code

















A note on indicator variables
You might notice that call only takes two values: 1 if the resume got a callback and 0 if it didn’t. So why are we treating it as an interval variable?
Variables coded 0-1 (also called indicator, dummy, or binary variables) have an unusual status. On the surface they look nominal, since they just sort observations into two categories. But because there are only two values, there is only one distance between them, and that distance is always the same: exactly 1. There’s no way for the spacing to be unequal, so the equal-intervals requirement is automatically satisfied.
This has a handy consequence: the mean of a 0-1 variable is the proportion of observations coded 1. When we take the mean of call, we’re getting the callback rate. A mean of 0.064 means 6.4% of resumes received a callback.
That’s why it’s reasonable to use a comparison of means here. We’re really comparing the proportion of callbacks between the two groups.

title: Linear Regression
text: We found a strong positive correlation between prison population and violent crime, but this does not license any claims about the size of correlation between prison population and violent crimes. For this we need to run a linear regression.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Regression vs Correlation

Units matter in a regression, they do not in a correlation
A regression is asymmetric: a regression of \(Y\) on \(X\) is different from a regression of \(X\) on \(Y\)

title: Linear Regression
text:
Interpretation

\(\hat{\alpha}\) is the intercept on the y-axis, the value that Y takes when X is zero. \(\hat{\alpha}\) is a constant, it doesn’t change and remains the same regardless of the value of X.
\(\hat{\beta}\) is the coefficient (or slope), the average change in Y for one unit increase in X. \(\hat{\beta}\) is always in terms of Y’s units.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Significance
Pr(>|t|) is the p-value. It’s the probability of getting a t-statistic at least as far from zero as the one we observed, if the null hypothesis were true. The |t| means it counts extreme values in either direction, so this is a two-sided test.
A small value means our result would be very unlikely if there were truly no effect, which gives us evidence against the null.

title: Linear Regression
text:
Reporting results






Result



Each additional prisoner per 100,000 people in the previous year is associated with an increase of 2.012 in the predicted violent crime rate per 100,000 people, which is statistically significant at the 95% confidence level.



Generic template

A one-[X’s unit] increase in [X] is associated with a \(\hat{\beta}\) [Y’s units] [increase/decrease] in [Y], on average. This estimate is statistically significant at the [95/99]% confidence level (\(\hat{\beta}\) = [coef], SE = [SE], p [= / <] [p-value]).

title: Hypothesis Testing
text:
Comparisons Allow us to Confirm a Hypothesis

Hypothesis Testing Procedure

Form a null hypothesis
Choose a test statistic
Ask whether observed value of a test statistic is likely to occur under sampling distribution of the null hypothesis

If likely, we fail to reject the null hypothesis
If unlikely, we reject the null hypothesis



In a comparison of Titanic passengers, first-class passengers had a different survival rate than third-class passengers.

Identify the null

\(H_0\) : The effect of being a first class passenger, rather than a third class passenger, on surviving the Titanic is zero.

Identify the appropriate test statistic

t-statistic of a two-sided two-sample t-test







t-test



A t-test, also known as a two-sample or difference-of-means t-test, tells us whether the difference between two group means is large enough that it’s unlikely to be due to random chance alone. It divides the difference in means by its standard error, so the resulting t-statistic measures how many standard errors apart the two groups are. The bigger the t-statistic, the stronger the evidence against the null. If you’re comparing means, think t-test.



We use a t-test when the independent variable splits the data into two groups and the dependent variable is interval.
Here, the groups are first-class and third-class passengers, and Survived is a 0-1 indicator variable, so its mean is the survival rate for each class. We’re asking whether the survival rate in first class differs from the survival rate in third class by more than we’d expect by chance.

Calculate the t-statistic










Code

Pull the groups we’re comparing into vectors first










- Use t.test()









Set p-value threshold
Look at the p-value

In the output from t.test(), the p-value is on the third line of the output, right after the t-statistic and degrees of freedom (t = ..., df = ..., p-value = ...)

Determine whether the results allow you to reject the null hypothesis

If the p-value is less than the threshold, you reject the null
If the p-value is greater than the threshold, you fail to reject the null

Reporting results







Result



First-class passengers had a survival rate 39 percentage points higher than third-class passengers (63% vs. 24%), a difference that is statistically significant at the 99% confidence level (t = 10.2, p < 0.001).



Generic template: [Group A] had a [difference] [higher/lower] [outcome] than [Group B] ([mean A] vs. [mean B]), a difference that is statistically significant at the [95/99]% confidence level (t = [t], p [= / <] [p-value]).


In a comparison of resumes sent out by Bertrand & Mullainatha, those that had White-sounding names were more likely to receive a call back than those with African-American sounding names.









Identify the null

\(H_0\) : A resume’s name sounding White instead of African-American does not increase the resume’s chance of getting a callback.

Identify the appropriate test statistic

t-statistic of an one-sided two-sample t-test







One-sided vs Two-sided t-test



We’re making a more specific claim than our Titanic example – we’re not just saying that some effect exists, we’re making a claim about both the existence and the direction of the effect, that White-sounding names get more callbacks, not more ar less. In this case, we use a one-sided t-test


Calculate the t-statistic










Set p-value threshold

We’ll use 0.05

Reporting results






Result



First-class passengers had a survival rate 39 percentage points higher than third-class passengers (63% vs. 24%), a difference that is statistically significant at the 99% confidence level (t = 10.2, p < 0.001).
